title: Mechanical Thoracic Spine Pain
lead: The thoracic spine is a common site of mechanical pain, and a common hiding place for serious disease.

blocks.text: The thoracic spine has 12 vertebrae, each joined to a pair of ribs. This rib attachment makes the region stiffer than the neck or lower back. Mechanical thoracic pain arises from the facet joints, costovertebral joints, discs or muscles, and changes with posture, movement and breathing. Thoracic pain is less common than neck or low back pain, and a higher proportion of thoracic pain comes from non-musculoskeletal causes (heart, lungs, aorta, abdominal organs, fracture, tumour) [Ref – to verify]. Therefore you must screen carefully before calling it mechanical.

items: Pain between the shoulder blades or along the spine, sometimes wrapping around the chest.
Worse with sustained sitting, twisting, deep breath at end range, or specific movements.
Eased by movement change or rest.
Local tenderness and stiffness at one or more segments.

blocks.label: COMMON STUDENT TRAP
body: "Pain is reproduced by palpation, so it must be musculoskeletal." Wrong. Serious pathology can coexist with local tenderness. A normal history is what reassures you, not a positive palpation.

rows: Does the pain change with movement, posture or position?
Is it related to exertion, and does it ease with rest within minutes?
Any breathlessness, cough, fever, coughing blood?
Is it linked to eating, indigestion, bowel or urine?
Any sudden tearing pain going through to the back?
Age over 50, cancer history, weight loss, night pain?
Osteoporosis, long-term steroids, minor fall or lifting?
Rash or burning along a band?
Morning stiffness for over 30 minutes in a young adult, improving with exercise?

items: Vital signs if any cardiopulmonary concern (heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature).
Posture and thoracic curvature (kyphosis, scoliosis).
Active movements: flexion, extension, rotation (best tested in sitting with arms crossed), side flexion.
Breathing: chest expansion; pain with deep breath.
Segmental palpation: central and unilateral PA pressures, rib springing.
Neurological screen if band-like pain or leg symptoms (thoracic myelopathy, root).
Cervical and shoulder screen.

sections.title: E. Special tests and examination findings

rows: Patient sits with arms crossed; actively rotates each way; therapist may add overpressure
Comparable pain with restriction supports a mechanical source
Prone; therapist's pisiform or thumbs over spinous process; gentle oscillation
Comparable pain and stiffness locates a segment
Prone or side lying; gentle anterior pressure over rib angle
Sitting slump with neck flexion and knee extension
Tape measure at the 4th intercostal space, full inhalation minus full exhalation
Reduced expansion may suggest axial spondyloarthritis or lung disease; compare with norms [Ref – to verify]
Movement-related, local stiffness, no systemic signs
Exertional or rest chest/back pain, sweating, breathlessness, risk factors
Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, fast heart rate, recent surgery or immobility
Sudden severe tearing pain, blood pressure difference between arms
Older, osteoporosis, sudden pain after minor load, height loss
Night pain, weight loss, cancer history
Burning band pain, rash after a few days
Related to meals, right scapular pain

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Chest or interscapular pain with sweating, nausea, breathlessness
Stop; emergency services; keep patient at rest
Sudden tearing pain, BP difference between arms, collapse
Sudden breathlessness, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, calf swelling
Cancer history, weight loss, constant night pain, age over 50
Band-like pain with leg weakness, gait change, brisk reflexes

steps: **Screen visceral and cardiopulmonary causes first** (questions plus vital signs).
**Any emergency feature?** Stop and call emergency services.
**Pain changes with posture and movement, comparable segmental signs, no systemic features:** working diagnosis mechanical thoracic pain.
**Treat** with manual therapy plus exercise; reassess after 2 to 3 sessions.

rows: Comparable stiff, painful segment; no contraindication
Supine (patient arms crossed, therapist's hand under the segment, thrust through the arms) or prone
Osteoporosis, fracture risk, fear, any flag
Prone, gentle oscillation at rib angle

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Thoracic extension over chair back or foam roller
Hands behind head, extend over the support, return
Side lying, knees bent, open top arm to the other side
Lie face down, raise arms in Y, T and W shapes

blocks.text: Heat for comfort; TENS optional. Other modalities are not routinely recommended.

items: Screen; educate about mechanical nature and good prognosis.
Manual therapy and mobility exercise early.
Strengthening and posture variety; ergonomic adjustments.
Self-management for recurrences.

blocks.text: Pain 0 to 10, rotation range (seated), comparable segmental sign, PSFS. New systemic symptoms override the plan.

blocks.label: CLINICAL CASE
body: A 52-year-old man reports pain between his shoulder blades for 2 days, 7/10, which came on while carrying shopping upstairs and eased after resting. He smokes and has high blood pressure. Palpation of T5 is mildly tender.

blocks.text: > Decision: this is not yet a mechanical diagnosis. Exertional onset, rest relief and cardiac risk factors require urgent medical assessment before physiotherapy.

items: **Why not treat T5?** The history suggests possible angina; local tenderness does not exclude it.
**Which vital signs would you take?** Heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, SpO2, temperature.
**What test distinguishes aortic dissection suspicion?** Blood pressure in both arms plus history of sudden tearing pain.
**A 70-year-old woman on long-term steroids has sudden thoracic pain after a sneeze. What do you suspect?** Osteoporotic vertebral fracture; avoid manipulation; refer for imaging.
**Why is thoracic pain more worrying than lumbar pain statistically?** A higher proportion has visceral or serious causes.

sections.title: Now You Should Be Able To

items: Screen thoracic pain for visceral and serious causes.
Examine thoracic movement and segmental mobility.
Choose safe manual therapy and exercise.
